findings.claim: Step 2 keeps top-level const cfg declarations in both src/a.js and src/b.js while Step 3 relies on node build.js to produce a working dist/bundle.js for Step 4 verification.
findings.evidence: build.js concatenates src/a.js and src/b.js directly with a newline and no scope wrapping. Both src/a.js and src/b.js declare top-level 'const cfg = require(...)'. The existing dist/bundle.js only avoids a collision because line 3 uses 'const cfg2' instead of 'const cfg'. Running node build.js after Step 2 will emit two top-level 'const cfg' declarations in dist/bundle.js and throw a SyntaxError ('Identifier cfg has already been declared') when loaded.
findings.evidence_reference: build.js line 3; src/a.js line 1; src/b.js line 1; dist/bundle.js lines 2-3
findings.repair: Before executing Step 2, decide either to rename 'cfg' in src/b.js (for example to 'cfg2' or inline the require) so concatenated declarations do not collide, or to include updating build.js to isolate each module scope before regenerating dist/bundle.js.

findings.evidence: The supplied repository files contain no existing test suite, so the checks in Step 4 are new, and the plan omits showing each check fail on a deliberately broken input (such as the unmodified files or a missing timeoutMs key) before showing it pass.
